---
title: "A first pattern: Zipf's law"
---

Word types in corpora tend to show a broad inverse relation between frequency and frequency rank. But computing rank and frequency from the same counts makes the two axes mathematically dependent, so the fitted relation is partly induced by the ranking operation.

We construct the rank–frequency curve, separate the tokens used to estimate rank from those used to estimate frequency, and then inspect the residual pattern that a fitted inverse curve leaves behind.

Piantadosi's (2014) [critical review](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-014-0585-6) demonstrates the problem with the written American National Corpus, separates rank and frequency estimation by splitting tokens, and shows systematic residual structure beyond a Zipf–Mandelbrot curve. The authorized ANC count snapshot is not available in this repository. We thus carry out an explicitly labeled, paper-aligned replication on [UD Turkish BOUN release 2.18](https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/tr_boun/), pinned at commit `0def94a229dcbc28d32192b0138b560c075c6d87` under CC BY-SA 4.0.

Türk et al. (2022) [describe the BOUN Treebank and its annotation](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-021-09558-0); Marşan et al. (2022) [describe later agglutination-sensitive revisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11782). The treebank contains written sentences from five Turkish National Corpus registers. Native-speaker linguists manually annotated and cross-checked automatically preprocessed sentences. The prepared table lowercases source surface forms with Turkish dotted and dotless I preserved, and it excludes punctuation, multiword-token range lines, and empty nodes while retaining component syntactic words. One row is one word-form type; `frequency` is its count among non-punctuation syntactic-word tokens. The immediate UD release permits redistribution under CC BY-SA 4.0, though the public documents do not independently expose the upstream Turkish National Corpus permission reported by the paper. The [data record](../data/ud-turkish-boun/README.md) gives the checksums and full terms caveat.

```{r}
#| label: load-turkish-frequencies
library(ggplot2)

forms <- read.csv("data/ud-turkish-boun/word-form-frequencies.csv",
                  fileEncoding = "UTF-8")

stopifnot(
  nrow(forms) == 33876L,
  sum(forms$frequency) == 104426L,
  !anyDuplicated(forms$word_form),
  all(forms$frequency > 0)
)

c(types = nrow(forms), tokens = sum(forms$frequency))
```

For each row, `word_form` is one lowercased surface type and `frequency` is the
number of retained syntactic-word tokens with exactly that form. For instance,
the most frequent row is *bir*, with 2,746 tokens; its count is a type-level <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
summary of token records, not 2,746 new word types. `nrow(forms)` thus
counts types, while `sum(forms$frequency)` recovers tokens.

## Rank and the descriptive model

Let $f(r)$ be the observed token count of the type assigned rank $r$. Zipf's law supplies the basic inverse form

$$
\widehat f(r)
\equiv
Cr^{-\alpha},
\qquad C>0,\ \alpha>0.
$$

The Zipf–Mandelbrot generalization shifts rank by $\beta$:

$$
\widehat f(r)
\equiv
C(r+\beta)^{-\alpha},
\qquad C>0,\ \alpha>0,\ \beta\geq 0.
$$

Here $f(r)$ is an observed count and $\widehat f(r)$ is a fitted count. The model is a descriptive approximation; matching it does not identify a mechanism of lexical choice, memory, or communication.

## Separate rank and frequency estimation

Following Piantadosi (2014), we use a fixed binomial token split. One count part assigns ranks and the other estimates relative frequency. The random split is a computational device applied to the observed Turkish counts, not a new linguistic dataset. It also does not repair sentence or register dependence because the aggregate table lacks document identifiers.

The 50/50 probability gives equal expected token totals to ranking and
frequency estimation. A more unequal split would estimate one side more
precisely at the other's expense. Within each type, `rbinom()` assigns every
observed token to the rank half with probability 0.5; the remainder enters the
frequency half. When rank-half counts tie, an independent uniform number gives
a deterministic ordering after the seed is fixed. Seed `20261018` is an
arbitrary reproducibility label, not a fitted quantity or a source of
independence.

```{r}
#| label: split-rank-frequency
set.seed(20261018)

forms$rank_count <- rbinom(nrow(forms), size = forms$frequency, prob = 0.5) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
forms$frequency_count <- forms$frequency - forms$rank_count

forms$tie_breaker <- runif(nrow(forms)) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
rank_order <- order(-forms$rank_count, forms$tie_breaker)
forms$rank_split <- integer(nrow(forms))
forms$rank_split[rank_order] <- seq_len(nrow(forms))

split_tokens <- sum(forms$frequency_count)
forms$relative_frequency <- forms$frequency_count / split_tokens

stopifnot(
  all(forms$rank_count + forms$frequency_count == forms$frequency),
  length(unique(forms$rank_split)) == nrow(forms),
  abs(sum(forms$relative_frequency) - 1) < 1e-10
)
```

We fit the curve as a multinomial model over the finite ranked inventory, following Piantadosi's analysis. For $V$ observed word-form types, the model assigns rank $r$ probability

$$
p(r\mid\alpha,\beta)
\equiv
\frac{(r+\beta)^{-\alpha}}
{\sum_{j=1}^{V}(j+\beta)^{-\alpha}}.
$$

If $n_r$ is the frequency-half count at rank $r$, maximizing the multinomial likelihood is equivalent to maximizing

$$
\ell(\alpha,\beta)
\equiv
\sum_{r=1}^{V}n_r\log p(r\mid\alpha,\beta).
$$

To see where this expression comes from, let $M=\sum_r n_r$. The multinomial
mass of the count vector is

$$
\mathbb{P}(\mathbf N=\mathbf n\mid\alpha,\beta)
=\frac{M!}{\prod_r n_r!}
\prod_{r=1}^{V}p(r\mid\alpha,\beta)^{n_r}.
$$

Taking logs yields a combinatorial term that does not depend on $\alpha$ or
$\beta$, plus $\sum_r n_r\log p(r\mid\alpha,\beta)$. Dropping only the constant
term gives the displayed optimization objective.

The ranks come from one half and the counts from the other, which removes the same-count error that Piantadosi identifies. Types with zero frequency-half counts remain in the model support even though they cannot appear on a logarithmic plot.

```{r}
#| label: fit-zipf-mandelbrot
log_sum_exp <- function(x) {
  x_max <- max(x)
  x_max + log(sum(exp(x - x_max)))
}

negative_log_likelihood <- function(theta) {
  alpha <- exp(theta[[1]])
  beta <- exp(theta[[2]])
  log_weight <- -alpha * log(forms$rank_split + beta)
  log_probability <- log_weight - log_sum_exp(log_weight)
  -sum(forms$frequency_count * log_probability)
}

zipf_fit <- optim(
  par = log(c(alpha = 1, beta = 2.7)), # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  fn = negative_log_likelihood,
  method = "L-BFGS-B",
  lower = log(c(alpha = 0.05, beta = 0.001)), # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  upper = log(c(alpha = 5, beta = 10000)), # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  control = list(maxit = 1000) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
)

zipf_coef <- exp(zipf_fit$par)
names(zipf_coef) <- c("alpha", "beta")
log_weight <- -zipf_coef[["alpha"]] *
  log(forms$rank_split + zipf_coef[["beta"]])
forms$fitted_frequency <- exp(log_weight - log_sum_exp(log_weight))

rank_frequency <- subset(forms, frequency_count > 0)
rank_frequency$log_residual <-
  log(rank_frequency$relative_frequency) -
  log(rank_frequency$fitted_frequency)

stopifnot(
  zipf_fit$convergence == 0,
  zipf_coef[["alpha"]] > 0,
  zipf_coef[["beta"]] >= 0,
  all(forms$fitted_frequency > 0),
  abs(sum(forms$fitted_frequency) - 1) < 1e-10
)

zipf_coef
```

The formula-to-code map is direct:

| Mathematical object | Code object |
|---|---|
| $r$ | `forms$rank_split` |
| $n_r$ | `forms$frequency_count` |
| $-\alpha\log(r+\beta)$ | `log_weight` |
| $\log\sum_j(j+\beta)^{-\alpha}$ | `log_sum_exp(log_weight)` |
| $-\ell(\alpha,\beta)$ | `negative_log_likelihood()` |

Optimizing `log(alpha)` and `log(beta)` enforces positive parameter values.
The starting values 1 and 2.7 are computational proposals, not assumptions
about Turkish. The wide bounds prevent invalid or numerically extreme searches,
and L-BFGS-B is chosen because it respects those bounds while using local
gradient information. Convergence code zero is necessary but not sufficient;
a production analysis should also compare starts and check whether the optimum
is away from the bounds.

The fitted exponent is `r round(zipf_coef[["alpha"]], 3)` and the fitted rank shift is `r round(zipf_coef[["beta"]], 3)`. These parameters describe this tokenization of this treebank release; they are not estimates for Turkish as a whole.

```{r}
#| label: plot-zipf-fit
#| fig-cap: "Turkish BOUN word-form frequencies. Ranks and relative frequencies are estimated from separate fixed token splits; the blue line is the fitted Zipf–Mandelbrot curve."
ggplot(rank_frequency,
       aes(rank_split, relative_frequency)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey") +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted_frequency),
            color = "#2C7FB8", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Frequency rank (rank split)",
       y = "Relative frequency (frequency split)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Inspect the residual structure

Define the log residual by

$$
e(r)
\equiv
\log f(r)-\log\widehat f(r).
$$

If the curve captured all systematic structure, residuals would fluctuate without an ordered pattern around zero. The restrained residual plot lets the data, rather than a callout, show where the approximation misses.

```{r}
#| label: plot-zipf-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Ordered residuals from the fitted Zipf–Mandelbrot curve. The horizontal line marks zero residual."
ggplot(rank_frequency, aes(rank_split, log_residual)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey") +
  geom_smooth(color = "#2C7FB8", method = "loess", formula = y ~ x,
              se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey25", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Frequency rank (rank split)", y = "Log residual") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The broad decline and the residual structure coexist. This is Piantadosi's description–explanation gap: a simple curve may summarize much of the distribution while providing weak evidence for any particular mechanism that can generate it.

This replication has two limits. First, BOUN is a five-register treebank, not a balanced probability sample of Turkish usage. Second, the aggregate frequency table permits a token split but not a document-level split, so discourse clustering remains. The result licenses a claim about represented word-form counts, not about a universal law of Turkish.

The [next page](possibilities-and-events.qmd) moves from the whole word-form inventory to an audited token extract and defines a finite probability experiment.

## Check your understanding

1. Use the visible code to identify the ten most frequent word forms and report their observed counts.
2. Recompute ordinary same-sample ranks from `frequency`. Why are those ranks mathematically dependent on the plotted frequencies?
3. Use `rank_frequency` to find the type with the largest absolute log residual. What does that residual establish, and what does it not establish about a generating mechanism?
4. Explain why lowercasing and excluding punctuation change both the type inventory and the rank assignment.
5. A student says that setting the seed makes the split counts independent of
   sentence and register. Which role of a random seed has been confused?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The ten most frequent forms are *bir* 2,746, *ve* 2,045, *bu* 1,258, *de* 836, *ki* 787, *da* 786, *için* 591, *çok* 485, *o* 450, and *gibi* 411. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Ordinary ranks are deterministic order statistics of `frequency`, so the plotted rank and frequency reuse the same counts and are mathematically dependent. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The largest absolute log residual belongs to *olanak* at split rank 32,474, with residual 3.119; this establishes that the fitted curve underpredicts that split count, not that any particular mechanism generated it. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Lowercasing merges case-distinguished strings, while punctuation removal deletes types and tokens; both operations change counts and thus the ordering that defines frequency rank. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. A seed reproduces the pseudorandom token allocation. It cannot restore
   document identifiers or remove dependence inherited from the corpus.

</details>

The Zipf analysis depends on keeping token counts distinct from type ranks. A
fixed split reduces the same-count rank error, though even a good descriptive
fit does not identify a linguistic mechanism. The [next
page](possibilities-and-events.qmd) moves from an aggregated type table to keyed
token outcomes and a finite probability experiment.
